paragraphs.text: A rolled [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) from 1980, now forty-six years old. Taiwan has a long habit of keeping oolong for years, called [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. Leaf chosen for keeping starts well roasted and dry, and keepers roast it again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in, since damp is what spoils a stored tea. No standard says how many years make an oolong old; those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty, and this one is well past both.

The record names only the island, which tells you the leaf was grown in [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label) and nothing about the mountain, township or height. Oolong came there with settlers from [Fujian](taiwan:history), who brought the plants and the craft, and by the nineteenth century the island was selling it abroad as Formosa Oolong. As a [partly oxidised](oolong:definition) tea, it sits between green tea and red tea.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
